title: Review into why pregnant woman moved hospitals three times while in pain
text:
Health authorities will review the care received by a pregnant Adelaide woman who was moved between three hospitals while experiencing "stabbing pain" before she required emergency delivery of her baby and an operation to repair a twisted bowel.

Kaitlin Jagu has received an apology from a senior health official after she said she received inadequate pain relief, and eventually lost consciousness in a hospital bathroom.

After experiencing abdominal pain on Tuesday, October 13, a 30-week Ms Jagu contacted Triple Zero (000) with the help of a colleague.

An SA Ambulance Service spokesperson said the patient was taken to the nearest hospital, the Royal Adelaide Hospital, as Ms Jagu's condition "was not initially considered to be directly related to her pregnancy".

"While at the Royal Adelaide Hospital, the patient was further assessed and redirected to the Women's and Children's Hospital (WCH)," the spokesperson said.

Ms Jagu told 891 ABC Adelaide while at the WCH, staff did tests "to determine the baby was OK".

Kaitlin Jagu was taken to two hospitals before she was transferred to Flinders Medical Centre. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

She said she was then taken to the Flinders Medical Centre (FMC), which was the only Adelaide hospital equipped to treat pregnant women with medical conditions that are not related to their pregnancy.

"There is only one hospital in this state that has the specialist expertise to look after sick pregnant women, and problems in the mum, and that is Flinders Medical Centre," Southern Adelaide Local Health Network executive director of medical services, Diana Lawrence, told 891 ABC Adelaide.

An emergency C-section

Throughout her transfers between hospitals, Ms Jagu experienced what she described as "burning, stabbing, consistent pain, shooting from my sternum down past my belly button".

Ms Jagu said when she arrived at FMC in the middle of the night, she was kept in an airlock room with a green whistle – a pain relief device – before being taken for tests.

She said FMC staff had tried to find the cause of her pain after first determining her unborn baby was safe.

Ms Jagu said when she tried to provide a urine sample, she passed out in the bathroom.

The woman said her loss of consciousness put her baby into distress, prompting an emergency caesarean section.

She said after her baby was delivered, doctors found her pain was caused by a twisted bowel, which was fixed during the surgery.

Kaitlin Jagu with her newborn baby. (Supplied)

Lack of communication

Ms Jagu said she had "an amazing experience within the birthing and assessment suite" and that nurses and midwives "did everything in their power to make me feel comfortable and safe".

But, she said the lack of communication to her, or her family, as officials tried to ascertain the cause of her pain were "big red flags".

"I'd want just clearer answers and better communication, and just an understanding of what was happening and what the next steps would be," she said.

"Although lots of things were happening in the background, it wasn't delivered to me. It was just very vague of 'this is what we need to do, wait and see'.

"Also, a clearer way to escalate concerns when a patient or their family feels that the situation is getting worse and we're not getting the answers that we need in the moment."

Dr Lawrence said she has since met with Ms Jagu to discuss her concerns, and that hospital and ambulance officials would convened for a review today.

"I apologised to her, absolutely, for a few things," Dr Lawrence said.

"Her pain relief wasn't managed adequately, but also apologised to her because we don't have many single rooms here at Flinders and they often have infectious patients.

"She actually was put into a bay, a mixed gender bay which is what we never want to do with [pregnant] women, and we rapidly put her into a side room as soon as one was available."

Ms Jagu said it was "great" the health authorities were addressing the issues she raised but she would like see change.

title: Victorian election to decide future of Melbourne wholesale market
text:
The Victorian Coalition plans to sell the Melbourne wholesale fruit and vegetable market if it wins the November state election.

The sale of the government-owned 67-hectare site at Epping, just off the Hume Freeway in the city's north, would be a key budget-balancing measure.

Meanwhile, Labor has ruled out a sale, meaning the market's future will be decided by the election.

Vendors at the market have had big rent increases in recent years. (ABC News: Joseph Dunstan)

Shadow Agriculture Minister Emma Kealy said the Coalition wants the market "back in the hands" of wholesalers or industry.

"This will raise around $600 million, which will help to pay down the state's debt that we're grappling with," she said.

"The leading markets in Australia that have gone down this pathway … government doesn't make for the best landlord when it comes to these sorts of businesses."

Market making a loss

The wholesale fruit and vegetable market moved to Epping in August 2015, following the closure of the previous decades-old market in West Melbourne.

It is the only wholesale trading centre in the state with 3,000 tenants selling fresh produce and cut flowers to independent retailers, hospitality businesses, aged care facilities, food processors and manufacturers.

An eight-month industrial dispute over rents ended in June 2025, when a new deal was agreed to by stallholders.

Emma Kealy says the sale would put the market back in the hands of wholesalers. (Supplied: Emma Kealy)

"The Melbourne wholesale fruit and veg market has been facing a lot of challenges over the past few years," Ms Kealy said.

"Unfortunately, the way … the statutory body of the Melbourne Market Authority was established, it has never been able to deliver a surplus.

"In fact, it's making about a $10 million loss every year.

"These wholesalers are just looking to be able to sell their fruit and their veg at a point which they're able to make a profit."

Michaela Settle says the sale would increase fruit and vegetable prices. (ABC News)

While the Coalition is using this pledge as a way to claw back debt, Labor is standing firm on its plan to keep the market.

"Victorians haven't even voted yet, and [Opposition Leader] Jess Wilson is already selling off our assets," Agriculture Minister Michaela Settle said in a statement.

"The Liberals are addicted to flogging everything off.

"Families are already doing it tough, and all this will do is make groceries more expensive, and leave farmers worse off."

Industry ownership opportunity

Vendor representative Fresh State has cautiously welcomed the Coalition's idea.

"It's an election promise I'd be happy to hear from either side, to be fair," Fresh State managing director and chief executive Jason Cooper said.

"For too long the market's been operated as a government-owned property asset rather than essential infrastructure supporting Victoria's fresh produce industry."

"It's a successful model that's been proven around the rest of the country that markets work better when they're run by people that actually know them."

Jason Cooper says he would welcome industry ownership of the market. (Supplied: Fresh State)

Mr Cooper disagreed with the government's assertion that shoppers and farmers would be worse off.

"I'm not sure how you could possibly make it any worse for them," he said.

"We don't simply want to see the government sell an essential piece of infrastructure to the highest bidder and walk away.

"We want a carefully structured transition that provides the industry with the opportunity to participate in its own ownership."

title: Last drinks for Boag's as final Tasmanian beers roll off production line
text:
The last Tasmanian-brewed Boag's beers were bottled in Launceston this morning, marking an end to 145 years of local production.

In the past century and a half, Boag's has cemented itself as a state icon and often run ads about being brewed with clean Tasmanian water.

The final bottles exited the assembly line this afternoon, ahead of the brewery shutting its doors for the final time on November 6, taking with it 42 local jobs.

Boag's will cease their Tasmanian operations in Launceston in November after 145 years of local operation. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

While the bottle production finished today, the final brewing day was in September.

Brewer Adrian Hinds, who has been a Boag's employee for 22 years, said it was an emotional day.

"To be honest, I'm holding it together; it's quite emotional," he said.

"Today was the last drop of Boag's put into containers; tanks are empty, everything's on a carton or pallet ready to go out to the public.

"Everyone was on the packaging line watching the bottles go through the labeller; it just shows what it means to the staff here.

" We love the place. "

Brewer Adrian Hinds has been a Boag's employee for over two decades. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Mr Hinds said for the last mashing, "everyone came up, got a sample of grain, put it in the mash tuns, so everyone had that final little touch on the last brew of draught that we did".

"After everyone left the brew house and I was in there by myself, I just sat there for a while and just listened to all the sounds, the pumps going and then sugar going in and then smelling the hops going in.

"To be here for the last fill, it's sad. I didn't think it would ever happen; it's a shame it's happening, but you can't control it."

"There was just that little bit of, 'Oh wow, I love this job and I'm gonna miss it so much,'" he said.

The Boag's Brewery site sits on the banks of the North Esk river in central Launceston. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Tasmania to start importing Boag's from mainland

Boag's has existed in Launceston longer than electricity.

Originally called the Esk Brewery, Scottish migrant James Boag and his son James Boag II began the operation in 1881.

Bottling machines in the brewery's early years. (Supplied: State Library and Archives Tasmania)

In 2008, Lion Australia, owned by Japanese beer giant Kirin, snapped up the brand for $325 million.

But in June, Lion announced an end to local brewing operations in Launceston, citing inflation and long-term declines in beer sales.

Brewing of the Boag's brand will continue on the mainland in New South Wales, Queensland and Victoria. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Most of Boag's brewing had already been moved interstate the previous year, leaving the Launceston operations running at one-fifth of its capacity.

The Boag's brand will continue to live on, being brewed in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland. Tasmania will now become an importer of its beverage icon.

Will the taste be different?

Boag's tour guide Phil Crowden has been taking visitors from around the world into the Boag's Brewery's inner sanctum for 17 years.

He said the skills of the local brewers were "unparalleled", but he had faith the mainland-brewed Boag's would still hit the spot for rusted-on fans.

James Boag beers can be found in every northern Tasmanian pub, bar and bottleshop. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"The technology's got so good at the moment," he said.

"I mean, breweries are making beers for other breweries around the world, and you can actually emulate the water from any particular place in the world."

An online petition was launched in a bid to try and stop the closure of the brewery. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Tasmanian water has long been lauded as the essential ingredient in Boag's, something the brand has heavily promoted in its advertising.

Mr Crowden said the exact mineral count of Tasmanian water would be replicated at the other breweries to get as close to the taste as possible.

A spokesperson for Lion said the company were considering whether the equipment from the Launceston site may be deployed to its other sites.

Decommissioning of the brewing equipment will begin after the November closure date and is estimated to take an additional 12 months.

Bestseller on tap at local pubs

Boag's is easily the bestseller at Launceston mainstay The Gunners Arms.

Publican Adrian Singline said Lion had indicated there would be no additional cost for the pub to stock Boag's when production moved thousands of kilometres interstate.

Adrian Singline owns Launceston pub The Gunners Arms and says Boag's has always been his top-selling product. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Mr Singline said the brewery's closure was a loss for the community and the tourism sector.

"You get tourists in, and the first two places you send them to are the Gorge and the brewery," he said.

He said his customers would be quick to tell him if they noticed a change in taste from the new batches.

The pure waters of Tasmania have been advertised as a key ingredient in the production of the local beer. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

What's next for the iconic site?

In July, Premier Jeremy Rockliff announced the Tasmanian government was interested in purchasing the historic Boag's site.

Well-known Launceston property developer Errol Stewart has helped drive that idea.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff (left) and property developer Errol Stewart (right). (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

His vision for the site includes a mix of commercial properties, a boutique hotel, large public open spaces, offices and car parking.

"There is a three-hectare opportunity which does not come along very often in any CBD of any city very often," Mr Rockliff said.

"This is an opportunity for huge economic potential in terms of private investment, jobs, hospitality and more."

An artistic render of what Boag's Brewery could look like after redevelopment. (Supplied: Errol Stewart)

Business Minister Felix Ellis said the Tasmanian government "continued to engage constructively" with Lion over the future of the site.

The Boag's Brewhouse, a taphouse and museum, will continue to operate beyond November, with a documentary cataloguing the final days of the brewery and its workers set to be released in the future.

title: How Antonelli can become F1's youngest world champion this weekend
text:
Italian F1 driver Kimi Antonelli has his first chance to win the world championship this weekend, as the 20-year-old closes in on a maiden title in just his second season.

The Mercedes driver has been a class above the rest in 2026, with eight grand prix wins and a further six podium places across 17 rounds.

This Monday's (AEDT) United States Grand Prix will be Antonelli's first match point where he can officially seal a championship that has felt like his for many months.

The equation for Kimi Antonelli is very simple: win and hope for other results.

Antonelli enters this weekend's grand prix on 340 points, 102 more than teammate George Russell and 111 ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

The Italian needs to have a lead of 125 points or more to seal the drivers' championship at the United States Grand Prix.

That will happen if Antonelli wins the race, Russell finishes ninth or worse, and Hamilton finishes fifth or worse.

Antonelli Russell Hamilton Championship result Win 9th or lower 5th or lower Antonelli becomes champion Win 8th or better 5th or lower Hamilton eliminated Win 9th or lower 4th or better Russell eliminated Win 8th or better 5th or lower Championship remains alive 2nd or lower Any Any Championship remains alive

After this weekend, there will be five grands prix left in the season — Mexico, Brazil, Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

There will be a maximum of 125 points left to win.

If Antonelli finishes exactly 125 points ahead of either Russell or Hamilton in Texas, mathematically either of those drivers could end the season level on points — if they won every race and Antonelli failed to score another point.

Even in that unlikely scenario, Antonelli would still become champion through a tie-break, having won more grands prix than the others.

title: Tech giant shares plunge 40pc after delays to Melbourne data centre
text:
Community opposition to one of Melbourne's largest hyperscale data centres has smashed the value of one of Australia's biggest companies.

A neighbourhood dispute over power poles has forced multi-billion-dollar tech giant NextDC to cut its net earnings and revenue forecasts by tens of millions of dollars, with a planned expansion hit with power supply and government approval delays.

The company, among Australia's largest 100 listed companies, notified the stock exchange this morning that its net revenue for the current financial year would be slashed by a third — now $475 million to $500 million — down from $615 million to $640 million.

The company's operating profitability was also revised down to $245 million to $265 million, from $385 million to $410 million.

Following this morning's announcement, NextDC's stock plummeted by 40 per cent.

NextDC attributed the revised estimates to delays to electricity network upgrades by energy supplier Jemena, required to increase power supply to its M3 data centre in West Footscray.

Located only 10 kilometres west of Melbourne's CBD, this data centre spans 41,000 square metres. (ABC News: John Gunn)

The West Footscray data centre, located just 15 metres from homes, has long been the subject of community opposition due to concerns over diesel and noise pollution.

The installation of towering power poles to accommodate the facility's vast electricity use became another flashpoint earlier this year.

In September, Jemena was forced to halt the installation of 15-metre-high power poles in Yarraville after being met with resistance from residents, several of whom blocked crews by leaving their cars and bins out.

The power poles can carry up to 66,000 volts of electricity, approximately 160 times the voltage of previous power poles.

Local councils and residents argued that they had not been adequately consulted over the upgrades.

The installation of power poles in Yarraville was met with fierce resistance from residents. (ABC News)

In its announcement to the ASX on Wednesday morning, NextDC said the delays meant the next grid supply for West Footscray was now not expected until 2028, deferring "the delivery and billing of contracted capacity".

"Jemena has advised NextDC that it has suspended parts of the network works required for the next increase in grid supply to M3 Melbourne," NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie said.

"We have taken the affected M3 contracts out of FY27 guidance until we can reliably estimate their contribution."

In a call with investors this morning, NextDC's group chief development officer Simon Cooper said the company was "exploring all avenues", including finding alternative locations for the power poles, or placing electrical cables underground.

"Undergrounding does take time and there's not an immediate option that we can work on now. But it is something that we are absolutely considering," Mr Cooper said.

Residents group renews calls for financial compensation

In March, NextDC applied to Victoria's planning minister under the government's fast-track Development Facilitation Program for the West Footscray centre to double in size to cover a 10-hectare parcel of land.

The company says that application has also been delayed until after the November state election, with the Victorian government "taking longer than expected".

Residents near data centre want compensation A Senate inquiry into artificial intelligence and data centres hears from residents and local councils about the impact of an influx of data centres in Melbourne's suburbs.

NextDC said it had put all new development projects and land acquisitions on hold for the foreseeable future and would evaluate capital recycling opportunities, including potential sales of selected development sites.

Local residents group Citizens of Tottenham welcomed news of the delays to the M3 data centre, describing it as a battle between David and Goliath.

“It's a significant moment for our area and a reminder that the people living beside these developments cannot simply be pushed aside,” the group's president, Jacqui Glover, said.

Fellow member Sean Brown repeated calls for impacted residents to receive remediation and financial compensation, including voluntary buybacks.

"NextDC M3 doesn't have social licence for the existing building, they certainly don't have it for an expansion," Mr Brown said.

"It's now up to NextDC to meaningfully respond to residents' remediation proposal. This lack of social licence won't change after 28 November and whoever forms government after then needs to respect this."

Sean Brown is a founding member of the Citizens of Tottenham. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

On Monday, the data centre operator asked the stock exchange to suspending trading in its shares, citing the need to provide a market update on the impact of the power supply delays.

The company's recent financial results noted a planned capital expenditure outlay of $1.3 billion, and stated that its West Footscray centre had a "total planned capacity upgraded from 200MW to 225MW".

Valued at close to $7 billion, NextDC has 17 operational data centres in Australia, with another nine in the development or planning stages.

Amid growing resistance to new data centres, the Victorian government announced new regulations to ban data centres near homes and schools, including 150-metre buffer zones, while mandating the use of renewable energy and non-drinking water.

Earlier this month, AI data centre company Firmus spectacularly withdrew its application to list on the ASX, after failing to gather sufficient investor interest.

title: Labor tension as Tasmanian MP calls for party 'that can win'
text:
Labor Leader Josh Willie says he "isn't going anywhere" as leader, despite tension caused by Braddon MP Shane Broad's social media posts.

Mr Broad, from the party's right faction, has stirred debate with his prolific online activity.

In a video posted on Monday, he said the parliament was in "chaos" and being "dictated to by the Greens and independents, who only really represent a minority of Tasmanians".

"Tasmania needs the parliamentary chaos to end and for the state to have a clear direction for the future," he said.

" It's about making a Labor party that can win a majority of seats in the parliament so that we can get stuff done. "

Mr Broad contested the party's leadership following the 2021 state election loss, but was strongly beaten by then-Labor member David O'Byrne.

It is not clear if Mr Broad would have the support of other MPs or rank-and-file members to challenge for the leadership.

Mr Willie told the media this morning he had spoken to Mr Broad on Tuesday, but did not reveal the content of that conversation.

Asked if he would still be the leader by the end of the year, Mr Willie said he wasn't going anywhere

"I'm focused on Tasmanians. I'm concerned about the debate happening in Tasmania at the moment," he said.

Mr Broad declined to comment.

Willie 'ambitious' for his party

The expansion of Tasmania's lower house to 35 seats has narrowed the possibility of either major party attaining majority government.

Labor has been out of power since the Liberals took government in 2014.

Labor currently holds 10 seats, having polled just 26 per cent of the total vote at the 2025 state election.

The Liberals are governing in minority with just 14 seats, despite collecting 40 per cent of the votes.

Leader Josh Willie says he's not going anywhere. (ABC News: Mitch Woolnough)

Following the election, the Liberals made overtures to the crossbench to win its support — including by promising to ban greyhound racing and review the salmon industry.

Labor, meanwhile, is seen as having improved its working relationship with the progressive side of the crossbench.

Josh Willie replaces Dean Winter as Tasmanian Labor leader Josh Willie will take over as Tasmanian Labor leader, a day after former leader Dean Winter moved an unsuccessful no-confidence motion in the Liberal government.

Mr Willie is understood to have told the Labor caucus earlier this year he wanted to see the party polling 30 per cent before the turn of the calendar.

However, last week he said that goal had changed because of the emergence of One Nation.

He told reporters today the party would continue to announce policies, having done so already.

"Policies like five-day kindergarten and universal access to three-year-old preschool will be a game changer for education; it will pay dividends for decades.

" I'm ambitious for the Labor Party. I want to see us return to government and that's what I'm working to do every single day. "

Liberal backbencher Michael Ferguson accused Mr Willie of distracting from his leadership woes.

"Whenever there is a decision to be made, a policy to be defended, Mr Willie hides," he said.

Apology demanded over Christmas scandal

Mr Willie held a press conference this morning to call on Premier Jeremy Rockliff to apologise for shaming a school's attempt to rename its Christmas celebration event.

"Premier Rockliff a few months ago said that culture wars frankly don't pay the rent," he said.

"He was right — yet a few months later he has taken a 180-degree U-turn."

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff's Facebook post critical of a school renaming an end-of-year Christmas event. (Facebook: Jeremy Rockliff)

In his original post, Premier Rockliff incorrectly asserted that there had been efforts made to "remove all references to Christmas in end of year school celebrations".

"Christmas wasn't being cancelled. He knew that; he misrepresented that, to participate in a culture war," said Mr Willie.

" Words matter when you're the leader of the state. His words have hurt a school community. "

Other conservative Liberal MPs, including Deputy Premier Guy Barnett, Treasurer Eric Abetz and Police Minister Felix Ellis, have all since posted, fanning the flames of the incident.

Tasmanian Treasurer Eric Abetz's AI-generated image he posted to Facebook on October 19, 2026. (Facebook: Eric Abetz)

Last night Mr Rockliff posted again to Facebook, defending his post.

"Christmas is part of our culture. It's part of our way of life," he said.

"I believe that I have a right to voice that opinion, on behalf of our community."

title: 'Happy, bubbly' young woman celebrated after death from rare condition
text:
Purple walls adorned with music posters and family photos, and a bed covered by her favourite My Little Pony blanket, are a colourful reminder of the impact Tori Punch made in her 24 years of life.

While the lights are off and the music no longer rings out from her bedroom, her mother Wendy Punch makes sure there is still music playing in the lounge room for her "happy, bubbly girl".

"Tori showed us how to be strong, [how] to get through it all," Wendy said.

Crystals and toys placed on Tori Punch's bed in memory of her. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

Tori died earlier this month after a long battle with Proteus syndrome, an extremely rare genetic condition that caused overgrowth of her bones, skin and tissue.

She was diagnosed at just 14 months old and, despite being unable to walk, she never let it stop her from enjoying life and pursuing her passions of singing and dancing.

"She had her carers all the time in there, doing karaoke with her in the room, dancing," Wendy said.

Tori celebrated her 24th birthday in May. (Supplied: Melinda Radburn)

Wendy said Tori was a big fan of celebrating birthdays and she remembered fondly one birthday during COVID, when more than 500 cars — including emergency services — showed their support.

Her last birthday — in May this year — was made special with a visit from her favourite local musician and a party that ended with a cake fight with her siblings.

Melinda Radburn and her mother Wendy Punch. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

"Tori was like my best friend," older sister Melinda Radburn said.

"I feel like Tori was the glue that kept us all together."

Rare condition

Proteus syndrome is an extremely rare, non-inherited mutation of the AKT1 gene, with fewer than a few hundred cases documented worldwide.

Tori loved karaoke and listening to music. (Supplied: Melinda Radburn)

Babies are typically born without apparent deformities, but symptoms appear in the first two years of life.

"With everything that the syndrome brought to her, she never let it impact who she was," her sister said.

In 2018, the family fought to get access to a medical trial from the US, which they were eventually granted, and Wendy said it was the reason Tori defied the odds to reach the age of 24.

Tori Punch celebrated her birthday with a visit from her favourite musician, Kerrilee Gallagher. (Supplied: Melinda Radburn)

"When Tori first got diagnosed with Proteus, we'd never heard of it in our life," she said.

"We had to do a lot of research to work out everything regarding the syndrome.

" Tori had been fighting for 24 years … she was the boss of it. "

An inspiring woman

A Facebook page moderated by her family has amassed more than 35,000 followers, many posting about how the young woman had inspired them.

"You touched my heart on how strong you were. I loved seeing yr [sic] video and photos of you smiling and singing," follower Tracy Horscroft said.

Wendy Punch says the messages of support for Tori brought her comfort. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

"I know I never met Tori but the updates on her page gave me smiles," Adele Pate said.

Her mother said the community response was overwhelming.

"A lot of feedback has come back, people telling us that, with Tori's page — that we've had going for around 15 years now — that it's given them inspiration to get up and do stuff," Wendy said.

" It's given me a lot of comfort, with a lot of the messages that have come through. "

"It shows that Tori didn't just genuinely have an impact on us, that she had a wider reach to so many people," Melinda added.

Her family said plans were being made to hold an open funeral the wider community could attend in Bundaberg later this month.

title: Australians run 80 hours or more in 'crazy' race with no finish line
text:
It sounds like a metaphor for torture: a running race with no finish line.

About 900 runners from 67 nations, including 15 Australians, crossed the start line of the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship at 11pm on Saturday AEDT at Kembla Grange in the New South Wales Illawarra.

In a deceptively simple test of physical and mental grit, each athlete completes a 6.7-kilometre course loop on the hour, every hour, until one runner remains.

They squeeze food and minutes of sleep into the remaining time, in an event that can stretch beyond four days.

Jonathan Ash was the first Australian to pull out, succumbing to injury on Monday afternoon after he exceeded the hour limit on his 41st lap.

He told the event's live stream that knee bursitis and muscle tightness from the 16th lap slowed him down.

"Basically every muscle in my body started to get knotted at some point," Ash said.

"We had to get a physio in to push that out.

"[It was] probably one of the most painful experiences of my life."

Jonathan Ash, 43, took up running in his 30s and is now one of Australia's top endurance athletes. (Supplied: Snapped Sport Pics)

The Shellharbour engineer is the second-ever Australian to complete 100 laps, equal to 670 kilometres, over four days in 2024, behind Phil Gore, who sits injured on the sidelines this year, tending to fellow athletes.

Gore broke the world record last year after running 119 laps, or 797.3km, after five days on a southern Queensland farm.

Each Australian runner has a team of supporters stationed in tents ready to provide first aid, food and water between loops. (Supplied: Snapped Sport Pics)

Melbourne's Brandon Lee Gretch tapped out after lap 73 about midnight on Wednesday and said he was proud of his effort, having achieved a personal best.

"I came in with 20 seconds to spare and had a shooting pain down my back. That was just killing me from about yard 67 onwards," he said.

"It was hell."

Brandon Lee Gretch, 32, described the world championship event as "running with 14 of my best friends". (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

The 32-year-old was cheerful as he snacked on chicken nuggets this morning with heavily bandaged feet.

"Myself as an eight-year-old would be so proud to know I got to put on the green and gold," Gretch said.

"It's weird because I am so sleep-deprived, I feel like my body automatically goes into recovery mode.

Dozens of local volunteers have helped coordinate the Backyard Ultra World Championship at the grassy Kembla Grange course. (Supplied: Snapped Sport Pics)

"The only bad thing is I always wake up [with] stiff legs, so I'll have to get moving again soon."

Backyard ultras were invented 15 years ago by Gary "Lazarus Lake" Cantrell and hosted at his Bell Buckle property in Tennessee.

"He wanted to challenge people to complete 100 miles in 24 hours," Australian race director Red Barnett said.

"It just grew in popularity as people pushed beyond the 24-hour mark.

"It is a bit of a crazy event."

Ash described the event as "the lesson that every person is incredibly capable of much more than they think they are".

"You don't know until you give it a shot," he said.

Dan Camac crossed the finishing line of lap 81 with about 10 minutes to spare on Wednesday morning, shortly after teammate Ben Nicholls. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Australian athletes have so far completed more than 1,000 laps, but the attrition rate has been severe.

"There's a mixture of fatigue, not getting their nutrition right, body ailments that are going on," Ms Barnett said.

"So unfortunately, we just had one after the other [drop out] and are left with two [Australian competitors].

" If all goes well, these guys [Dan Camac and Ben Nicholls] are hoping to get to 100 hours, which is Thursday morning. "

Red Barnett started hosting Backyard Ultras in Wollongong's south in 2020 and is now managing the Australian course of the World Championship. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

Ms Barnett said things would become "drastically harder" for the remaining Australians.

"When there is only two left, they really need to work together," she said.

"Having a lot of people around to support and cheer them on, even through the nights, all that really helps, but it's going to be a huge mental test."

title: RBA deputy warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' as next decision looms
text:
Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser says the inflation outlook is "materially worse" than the RBA had forecast, raising the prospect of another interest rate hike as soon as November.

Just under a fortnight out from the next interest rate decision, Mr Hauser warned high inflation was becoming entrenched in the Australian economy.

"We are beginning to see some signs that some people in the community are not sure if we're going to bring inflation back into target at all, or certainly not for an extended period," Mr Hauser told the Citi Investment Conference in Sydney.

The RBA targets headline inflation between 2 and 3 per cent on average over time.

Inflation currently sits at 4 per cent, according to the August consumer price index.

Mr Hauser said the central bank's liaison program and surveys showed there was "an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that, maybe, sort of 3 per cent, 3.5 per cent [inflation] is the new normal".

"Look, that is the central banker's nightmare.

"We can't allow expectations to shift away from target."

Market pricing now puts the chance of an interest rate hike in November at 51 per cent, based on Bloomberg data.

The odds of a hike next month had dipped below 20 per cent last week, after the unemployment rate reached a five-year high in September.

UBS chief economist George Tharenou described Mr Hauser's remarks as "hawkish" and said the investment bank was forecasting a November rate hike.

"Hauser's comments today are consistent with our view of the likelihood the RBA staff provide an explicit recommendation at the November meeting to raise the cash rate," Mr Tharenou said.

The RBA will release its quarterly forecasts in its Statement on Monetary Policy on November 3, the same day the interest-rate-setting board next hands down a decision.

Betashares chief economist David Bassanese agreed that the RBA official was setting the stage for a Melbourne Cup day hike.

"Despite the steadfast claims that the Reserve Bank is no longer in the business of offering forward guidance, its signals to the market in recent weeks have rarely been clearer," Mr Bassanese said.

" In short, the RBA seems increasingly prepared to risk a recession to get inflation down – given it has been above target for an extended period and it is sensing evidence of rising inflation expectations within the community. "

"It remains possible the RBA board vote will be split, and the external members have a majority to hold rates, and hence effectively 'outvote' Bullock and Hauser," Mr Tharenou said.

However, even if the RBA holds rates in November, he still would expect "a 'hawkish hold', with the RBA retaining a tightening bias … and also setting up a hike at the subsequent meeting in December".

'Laying shorter-term pain on top of pain'

Mr Hauser reiterated the "hard choices" facing the RBA as it balanced the pressures on prices from the Middle East crisis, the AI and technology boom and weak productivity growth.

Asked about the pain of higher interest rates hitting many households, on top of cost-of-living pressure, the deputy governor said: "It's a continuous challenge to explain this."

"The reason is that, even though we are laying shorter-term pain on top of pain, it's to prevent a longer and potentially far worse pain down the track if inflation expectations get locked in," Mr Hauser said, echoing comments RBA governor Michele Bullock has made as the central bank has lifted rates.

The RBA and the inflation myth The Reserve Bank doesn't want consumer prices to come down, but to rise more slowly. It's a common misunderstanding that the ABS is partly responsible for.

Mr Hauser downplayed concerns about the state of the jobs markets, saying there was potentially "noise" in the numbers, after the unemployment rate rose to 4.7 per cent in September.

"That said, it clearly was a little weaker than we and others have been expecting," he said.

"I stress the 'little'. These unemployment numbers in Australia are still right at the bottom or very near the bottom of G20 out-turns on labour markets."

He said "no lost job is one to celebrate" but the labour market needed to soften.

"We need to see some easing in the economy, whether [the unemployment rate] goes to 5 [per cent], whether it goes to some other number," Mr Hauser said.

"That's a debate we're having in the context of our forecast at the moment, and you'll see our answers to that in a week or two."

title: Chinese student deported from Taiwan after controversial 'pinching' video
text:
An exchange student from China has been deported from Taiwan after posting a controversial video of himself using an illusion technique to make it look like he is pinching the Taiwanese president.

Lai Ching-te was speaking at the National Taiwan University last week when the student, identified publicly via his surname Wang, filmed the president from the audience.

Wang used an optical illusion technique, forced perspective, and put his fingers in front of the camera so it looked like he was pinching the president.

In the caption of the video posted on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Wang wrote: "Lai Ching-te is right here. Isn't it your once-in-a-lifetime opportunity."

The Chinese exchange student was deported from Taiwan on October 16. (Supplied: National Immigration Agency)

He also tagged the post with "cross-strait reunification", "oppose separatist acts seeking Taiwan independence" and "reunification is inevitable", in phrases which often appear in Chinese political rhetoric.

Wang has since deleted the video, apologised, and all content on his Douyin account has been cleared.

China sees the self-ruled island of Taiwan as part of its territory and has vowed to take it back.

Labelled as a separatist by Beijing, Mr Lai has repeatedly said the Republic of China (Taiwan) is a sovereign and independent country.

On October 16, the National Immigration Agency of Taiwan confirmed the student had been deported after his Taiwan entry permit was revoked.

This was due to violating the "principle of equality and dignity", part of regulations governing mainland Chinese people's entry into Taiwan, the agency said.

The student has been banned from entering Taiwan for five years.

"Our country is [a] democratic, free, and pluralistic society, respecting different opinions and normal exchanges; however, people from mainland China coming to Taiwan must still comply with our laws and related regulations," the agency wrote in a statement.

The post on Chinese social media included tags like "cross-strait reunification". (Douyin)

The National Taiwan University told the ABC the deported student was from a partner university, and it provided all necessary assistance during the authorities' inquiry.

"We respect differing opinions on public policies, as rational dialogue is the cornerstone of a democratic society," a university spokesperson said.

"We hope this incident serves as a reminder that the exercise of free speech must always come with mutual respect for others."

Local media reported that Kuomintang (KMT) politician Lin Pei-hsiang questioned the deportation decision, asking whether deporting the student over a social media post infringed on freedom of speech.

He suggested that political satire should be differentiated from a real threat.

Lo Wen-jia, secretary-general of Taiwan's Straits Exchange Foundation, said he respected the decision of the immigration agency, but he hoped that the incident would not affect future mainland exchange students to Taiwan.

The ABC has approached the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Australia and the Chinese embassy for comments.

title: Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with MS
text:
Christina Applegate has revealed her doctor says she does not have multiple sclerosis (MS) and was misdiagnosed.

The actor, known for hits like Anchorman, Married With Children and Dead to Me, said she continued to suffer debilitating symptoms.

“I’m back at square one where I don’t know what’s going on with me," she said in the latest episode of her podcast, Messy.

Christina Applegate's MS-related depression Actor Christina Applegate has opened up on a podcast about feeling down as a result of what she has to deal with day-to-day as someone living with Multiple Sclerosis.

Applegate announced on social media in 2021 that she had been diagnosed with MS and described how she had been on a "strange journey".

"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden I'm better," she told her Messy podcast co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler of Sopranos fame, who has lived with multiple sclerosis for more than two decades.

Applegate said the news had put her in an odd place because she, along with Sigler, had become prominent advocates for people with MS.

"It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down,” she said.

" It's very unnerving, and it's really confusing for me. "

MS is an autoimmune neurodegenerative disease that affects nearly 3 million people worldwide and can be difficult to diagnose, leading to misdiagnoses in a fifth of cases, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

California-born Applegate had previously described dealing with difficulty walking and balance problems, as well as a lack of coordination and numbness in her extremities.

But she said the diagnosis had provided some clarity and a path forward, whereas having no explanation for her symptoms left her once again searching.

"It's hard to say, but she [the doctor] came into my room and she said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,'" Applegate said.

"I was like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.

"I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to the doctor's office. I can't walk from the car to the room."

title: PNG Chiefs unveil new logo ahead of 2028 NRL entry
text:
The PNG Chiefs have unveiled the club's inaugural logo ahead of its debut NRL season in 2028.

The club says the striking logo, designed by a team of graphic artists in Papua New Guinea, depicts what makes the Chiefs "strong and what makes us unique".

A supporters' jersey was also unveiled on Wednesday.

The new logo and jersey were described as a defining moment for the new club as it prepares to enter the NRL, based in a nation which is obsessed with rugby league.

PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said the unveiling of the logo marked "one of the most significant milestones in the journey of the PNG Chiefs".

"This is the first time that our club has its true, complete identity — a logo and jersey that our players, partners and fans can hold to as their own," McPherson said.

"The logo of the PNG Chiefs tells a story about Papua New Guinea — our people, what makes us strong and what makes us unique.

"The jersey of the PNG Chiefs is more than what players wear when they take to the field; it is a symbol of belonging, unity and the opportunity to represent millions of Papua New Guineans on the national stage.

"We know the responsibility that comes with establishing this club and we are incredibly proud to show our club to the world today.

"We strive for the PNG Chiefs to be something our country is proud of in every way — not because of the success that we will achieve on the field, but for the opportunities and legacy we will create for our country."

Elements of the PNG Chiefs logo

As per the PNG Chiefs media release

The feather headpiece: Inspired by Papua New Guinea's ceremonial plumes, the five feathers represent strength, beauty, chiefly status and national pride, with the Southern Cross connecting the club to the nation's flag.

The cassowary bone: Inspired by warrior traditions, the cassowary bone symbolises chiefly status, courage, power and the fighting spirit of the team.

The face: The chief's face represents the shape of Papua New Guinea, with ceremonial red paint showing a nation united through one warrior, one team and one purpose.

The kina shells: Representing traditional wealth, trade and prestige across Papua New Guinea's coastal, island and highland communities, the kina symbolises the value, legacy and future the club is building for the nation.

title: Snooker player in tears, hugged by presenter, after emotional and raw interview
text:
Former world number one snooker player Mark Allen has given an emotional and tearful interview, which involved a hug from the presenter and the admission that he may give up the game.

Allen, 40, took a break from playing after losing a dramatic semifinal in April's World Snooker Championship in April.

The Northern Irishman is understood to have taken time away from the game to deal with private matters, and it has cast doubt over the 40-year-old's future in the sport.

Loading Instagram content

Allen returned to the table for the first time since the world championship semi, where he missed a match-ball black that would have sent him to the decider, with a 4-2 defeat in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open to good friend Jordan Brown.

After the defeat, Allen did an interview with TNT Sports presenter Rachel Casey, where he admitted he was strongly considering throwing away the game he loved.

"I'm in a bad place at the minute, so even just to go out there and try was tough," Allen said.

"I think if I weren't playing Jordan, I wouldn't have come back.

"I felt like if I was going to play one last time, playing here at the Waterfront, where it all started in 2005, against one of my best mates — I thought that was a better way to sign out."

Asked if he was genuinely considering retirement, the winner of 12 ranking tournaments said it was a real possibility.

"I've been flooded with support but the problems are within. I just don't see a future with snooker in it, if I'm honest," he said.

"It's sad to say, because it's all I've loved to do since I was 12, but the last few months has been really difficult, and it's put snooker into perspective for me. At the minute, I'm just trying to survive."

In a touching moment, the interview was paused as Casey gave a clearly distraught Allen a comforting hug.

Allen also gave an interview with BBC Sport NI, where he said he was not prepared to retire now, but he had contemplated it "for a while".

Allen is a former world number one with 12 ranking titles in his career since turning professional in 2005.

He has won his home Northern Ireland Open twice, as well as two of the three Triple Crown events — Masters (2018) and the UK Championship (2022).

Loading Instagram content

Brown, who advances to the final 32 in Belfast with his win, described the match against his friend Allen as " the hardest match I've ever had to deal with".

"I don't even know what to say, I'm lost for words," he told Casey on TNT Sports.

"I've missed him, I love him. Just a great guy, through and through."

title: Black beats brown as marketing changes the makeup of Australian cattle herd
text:
It may seem like a fickle fashion trend, but as far as the Australian cattle industry is concerned, brown is out and black is in.

Just ask Stephen and Jodi Peake, who, after six decades of breeding Hereford cattle in north-west New South Wales, are selling off their entire herd.

The two have spent years perfecting their stock and genetics, broken weight-gain records with their steers and even once sold a prize bull for more than $60,000.

Stephen and Jodi Peake from the Bowen Pastoral Company based in Gunnedah and Barraba. (ABC New England: Juno Robertson)

But as the Peakes near retirement, they have decided to focus on two of their other breeds: Angus and Wagyu.

"Angus are a worldwide popular breed. They tick a lot of boxes for the end consumer as well as the producer," Mr Peake said.

"Every breed has their day in the sun."

Angus were a minority breed 30 years ago. (Supplied: Stephen and Jodi Peake)

An Angus boom

Hereford cattle were first brought to Australia 200 years ago and have historically dominated its beef industry.

In 1990, farm survey data from the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences showed the breed was the country's most popular, making up just over a quarter of the national herd.

By comparison, Angus cattle were just over 4 per cent.

Fast forward 35 years and the black cattle breed has surged in popularity through savvy marketing, fast-food branding and export markets.

Charles Boog says that, based on available information, Angus beef has become dominant. (Supplied: Charles Boog)

According to a recent Meat & Livestock Australia (MLA) survey, Angus led national herd growth between 2023 and 2025, gaining 1.76 million head.

Market analyst Charles Boog said it was difficult to accurately study long-term breed preferences in Australia because there is no mandate to record cattle breeds at saleyards.

But looking at a "patchwork of information", one thing is clear: Angus has taken the lead.

"As one indicator of current breeding demand, [trade publication] Beef Central recorded 11,328 Angus bulls sold at auction in 2025 compared with 1,780 Herefords," he said.

More money, more marketing

Brad Hine from peak body Angus Australia said the breed's success was partly a marketing story.

The Angus name strengthened in 1995 when the association established guidelines for a verified label.

Beef exports to Japan also grew significantly through the 90s, with the foreign market offering a premium for black cattle.

"Verified Angus Beef" must contain a minimum of 75 per cent Angus-breed content with no dairy characteristics. (Supplied: Stephen and Jodi Peake)

McDonald's premium-branded Angus products, marketed globally from 2009 until June this year, also helped establish the breed as a known commodity.

Dr Hine said sale data from AuctionsPlus showed farmers now made more money per head on Angus cattle.

The nation's Angus herd grew by an estimated 1.76 million head between 2023-2025. (Supplied: Stephen and Jodi Peake)

A mixed cattle future

Herefords Australia chief executive Hamish Chandler said despite a historical departure from the breed, the association's membership numbers have stabilised over the past five years.

He said he was confident the breed would play a critical role into the future, as genetic research improved.

"Over the last two to three years, the number of Hereford cows in the national breeding herd has increased by around 26 per cent," he said.

Hamish Chandler says there is still a role for Herefords. (ABC New England: Juno Robertson)

Agriculture consultant Alastair Rayner said Australia's cattle breed mix would likely stabilise around where it is today, with a possible "increase in tropically infused cattle" in the future.

The MLA survey pointed to a similar trend, with Santa Gertrudis and Droughtmasters the second and third fastest growing herds, respectively.

Both are crossbreeds with European and Indian origins.

Crossbreeds like the Droughtmaster are gaining in popularity. (Supplied: Droughtmaster Australia)

Mr Rayner said unlike in the past, "there's never going to be just one breed" dominating the industry, as different environments call for different types of cattle.

"Rather than choosing a breed and trying to make everything fit, work out what you need and find the breed that best fits you," he said.

Red Metal has kicked off a crucial phase of metallurgical testwork at its Sybella rare earths project in Queensland, launching six-metre-tall column leach tests designed to simulate a full-scale, low-cost, heap leach operation for its multi-billion tonne monster. The program marks a significant de-risking milestone for the project, providing the most realistic data yet on recoveries, acid consumption and processing kinetics ahead of a planned definitive feasibility study (DFS) on what some resources pundits are calling the Escondida of rare earths. Red Metal has commenced six-metre-tall column leach tests to simulate a commercial-scale heap leach for its giant Sybella rare earths project in Queensland. The new tests are being run on slightly weathered rock and transitional ore from Sybella’s Kary Zone deposit, which sits just 20km south of the major mining hub of Mount Isa. The company plans to load -20mm crushed ore into 150mm-diameter columns standing six metres high to closely replicate the conditions of a commercial heap leach pad. In heap leaching, a chemical solution is trickled through the crushed ore to dissolve the valuable metals, which are then collected from the liquid and recovered.

‘(This) next step far more closely replicates the compaction, percolation and acid distribution inside a full-scale commercial heap leach.’ Red Metal managing director Rob Rutherford The final validation is expected to build on Red Metal’s previously successful two-metre column program that delivered impressive neodymium extraction of up to 76 per cent and praseodymium extraction of up to 78 per cent from transitional ore. Red Metal managing director Rob Rutherford said: “This important next step far more closely replicates the compaction, percolation and acid distribution behaviour we expect inside a full-scale commercial heap leach.” The prize for Red Metal is a low-cost processing route for what is a geologically unique and potentially globally significant mineral deposit. The company has already defined a monster 4.795-billion-tonne inferred resource at Sybella, where the sheer scale and potential for zero-strip mining make bulk-tonnage processing methods such as heap leaching an attractive option for unlocking economic value. In a concurrent program, the company has also started a series of two-metre column tests to assess a coarser -30mm crush size. Proving that a coarser grind can still deliver strong recoveries could be a game-changer for the project’s economics, materially lowering crushing costs and potentially allowing higher stacking heights on the leach pads, further reducing expenditure.

While Sybella is its flagship, Red Metal has also kicked off a new “Big Copper” exploration strategy, targeting giant iron-oxide-copper-gold (IOCG) discoveries in Queensland’s north-west minerals province, analogous to the nearby Ernest Henry and Osborne deposits. The company recently expanded its copper hunt, lodging 17 new tenement applications around its Gulf and Three Ways projects and is now planning two fully-funded drill holes to test targets at both projects, with the Gulf hole partly funded by a $200,000 Queensland Government grant. As Red Metal sharpens its copper hunt in Queensland’s far north and Sybella’s near-5-billion-tonne resource edges towards economic studies, cracking the rare earths processing puzzle could prove the key to unlocking the project’s enormous potential. Bonnie Garmus’ sprightly second novel has much in common with her first, the irresistible 2022 bestseller Lessons in Chemistry (which she published at the age of 65). Both deal with the pressures of the workplace, the rejections, resentments and ridicule, and both are flavoured by the same delicious screwball spirit that gave so much zest to so many zany Hollywood comedies of the 1930s and 1940s. Films such as Bringing Up Baby, Palm Beach Story, Ball of Fire and The Major and the Minor. Like them, the two books feature eccentric, expansive supporting casts whose wackiness embodies the mad, mad, mad, mad world we all have to deal with. And just as dogs frequently play key roles in those films, they’re also pivotal in Garmus’s novels: Elizabeth’s Six-Thirty in the first, and Batter, who doesn’t actually appear in Peck & Peck but whose history has a significant role to play and whose name has been bestowed on the central character and narrator. Author Bonnie Garmus. Peter Rae Even more substantially, both books are touched by the tenor of the times in which they’re set. For Lessons in Chemistry, it’s the 1960s as the set-upon Elizabeth takes a stand against a patriarchal order that would have her trapped on the sidelines. In Peck & Peck, it’s the 1980s, as the timeworn struggle between business and the arts rears its ornery head once more inside the eponymous publishing company and against a background of technological change. A key difference between the books is that, whereas the first is written in the third person, surveying its female protagonist’s situation and circumstances from the outside, the new one places us inside its male protagonist’s tortured efforts to understand the forces that have shaped his life and, in his words, “to generate the one thing (he) craved more than anything: respect”.

Advertisement

We gradually come to recognise that, while Batter is well-armed for his encounters with the world – he has a lot of data on tap, much of it gleaned from his type-designer mother and historian father – there’s much about it that he doesn’t understand. Alongside this, it becomes clear from his dealings with others that his instincts are more trustworthy than his actions. As the book begins, he’s in prison. All that follows provides an explanation, his explanation, for how he ended up there. It’s an ingeniously complicated route that begins with his family history and becomes especially convoluted when he bluffs his way into a job at Peck & Peck. An esteemed poetry quarterly boasting an editorial staff of 39 and based in an awe-inspiring building in New York, it’s currently under the sole management of Salton Peck. He’s taken charge after a falling-out with his twin brother, Declonius. As its title suggests, the book’s founding principle is the idea that nothing can be viewed in isolation, that everything has its double, a shadow side. The Peck & Peck building seems like a sanctuary when nobody’s around and a madhouse when they are. The Peck brothers, the third generation of twins to head the company, are mirror opposites. The idealistic Declonius, a champion of the arts, oozes contempt for the dunderheads of the world who don’t appreciate their importance. Of his brother, an abrasive, pontificating businessman, he says, “If he can’t quantitatively measure something’s value, then it’s worthless.” Twins are part of Batter’s family history too. He’s haunted throughout by the one with whom he shared their mother’s womb and who didn’t survive, and his divided inner life comes to mirror the conflict between the Peck brothers. In the light cast by the book’s refutation of black and white certainties about anything, it’s clearly not by chance that his surname is Gray. Or that there’s much more to his mother’s preposterous stories about the dog he’s been named after than he (and we) initially realise.

Advertisement

Garmus established herself as an astute and witty social satirist with Lessons in Chemistry and those qualities are again in evidence here. Peck & Peck is admirably sharp in its depiction of how companies operate as a matter of course, riven by divisions, uncertainties and secrets at the same time as they provide opportunities for growth and adventure. It’s also hugely appealing in the empathy it shows for those hapless souls immersed in a maelstrom that seems to be denying them the respect they believe they deserve. Orbit Resources has struck a geological sweet spot at its Lewis Ponds gold-silver and base metals project in NSW’s prolific Lachlan Fold Belt, visually identifying 11.8 metres of massive and semi-massive sulphides in drilling - the host rock for rich concentrations of its valuable polymetallic mineralisation. The standout hit included a 3.55-metre section, estimated at a whopping 50 per cent massive sulphides from 255m downhole, suggesting roughly half the rock is made up of sulphide minerals. Those sulphide minerals can contain substantial concentrations of zinc, lead and copper – with some carrying up to 86 per cent of their respective base metal by weight – alongside the potential for valuable gold and silver credits. Orbit Resources’ Lewis Ponds project, 15km east of Orange in New South Wales. The company says its latest sulphide-packed hole was drilled at the well-understood Tom’s Lode, with visual estimates suggesting the sulphide assemblage is dominated by pyrite (iron sulphide), followed by sphalerite (zinc), galena (lead) and chalcopyrite (copper). The hit also included 4.2m of 25 per cent semi-massive sulphides from 255.3m, followed by the 3.55m massive sulphide zone. Although the initial observations are considered encouraging, assays will have the final say. Core is now being prepared for testing, with results expected in the December quarter.

‘Drill hole 12 has intersected a substantial zone of visually identified semi-massive to massive sulphides at Tom’s Lode.’ Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens Orbit’s current diamond drilling program at Lewis Ponds is designed to increase confidence in the project’s existing substantial mineral resources and provide material for future metallurgical testwork, which will ultimately support economic studies for production. Three holes totalling 1168.8m have already been completed, with a final 300-metre hole currently in progress targeting its Spicer’s Lode to the deposit’s north. Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens said: “Drill hole 12 has intersected a substantial zone of visually identified semi-massive to massive sulphides at Tom’s Lode, broadly where predicted by our geological model. While assays are pending, the intersections provide further confidence in our geological interpretation.” Away from the drill bit, the company recently fired the starting gun on a spin-off of its Narraburra rare earths project in central NSW into a new, dedicated ASX-listed vehicle called Matrix Critical Minerals.

Advertisement

In a clever piece of corporate work, the initial public offering (IPO), which is seeking to raise up to $12 million, allows Orbit to crystallise the value of a promising but non-core asset while sharpening its focus on its core business: unlocking the potential of its gold, silver and base metal assets in the prolific Lachlan Fold Belt. Orbit’sLachlan Fold Belt portfoliois anchored by the advanced Lewis Ponds gold-silver project just 15 kilometres east of Orange, which hosts a formidable existing resourceof 17.52 million tonnes grading 1.12 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, 53.34g/t silver, 2.06 per cent zinc, 1.10 per cent lead and 0.14 per cent copper. This equates to a combined 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent, including an impressive 630,000 ounces of gold and 30.1 million ounces of silver. The mineralisation is classified as a volcanic-hosted massive sulphide (VMS) system, with the primary mineralisation extending over a 1200-metre-long zone. With the rods now spinning on the final hole of the current campaign, management is turning its attention to completing the program, interpreting the pending assays and selecting drill core for metallurgical work. The company also expects to complete its analysis of high-resolution drone magnetic data collected near its recent Cousin Jack discovery this month. With a hefty resource already in the bag, drilling wrapping up to feed into prefeasibility work and a corporate deal streamlining its portfolio, Orbit has plenty brewing. Now it’s over to the lab to see whether those shiny cores are hiding a bonanza - because rose-tinted geology is one thing; the assays are where the rubber hits the road. AP Stocks wavered in the morning, then turned south after RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said Australia’s inflation outlook looks “materially worse” than the central bank predicted in August, citing higher oil and technology prices and persistent domestic price pressures. “We’re seeing higher AI prices, tech prices feeding through into CPI,” Hauser said during a fireside chat on Wednesday, responding to a question about the prospects for a rate hike at the RBA’s policy meeting in early November. Oil prices are about a third higher than the RBA had assumed, with fewer fiscal interventions cushioning the impact on consumers, he added.

Sarytogan Graphite has unveiled a cracking definitive feasibility study (DFS) for the upstream component of its mammoth graphite deposit in central Kazakhstan, outlining a low-cost, long-life operation with a pre-tax net present value (NPV) of US$132.7 million (A$189.6M) using an eight per cent discount rate. The initial 50,000-tonne production profile is slated for three distinct markets. The company plans to sell 20,000 tonnes annually into the drilling fluids, lubricants and friction products markets, with another 10,000 tonnes of unclassified concentrate aimed at the foundry and iron recarburizer sector. Sarytogan Graphite’s proposed 50,000tpa processing plant at its graphite project in Kazakhstan. The remaining 20,000 tonnes will be earmarked as feedstock for Sarytogan’s own planned downstream business, designed to produce high-value ultra-high purity fines and coated spherical purified graphite for the burgeoning advanced battery market. The study maps out a graphite concentrate operation requiring a relatively modest capital outlay of just US$80.5 million (A$114.86M). The project is forecast to deliver a solid pre-tax internal rate of return (IRR) of 19.8 per cent and a healthy earnings before tax and depreciation (EBITDA) margin of 51 per cent, based on the average selling price of US$805 (A$1148) per tonne. The company says this is underpinned by an exceptionally low operating cost of just US$364 (A$519) per tonne of concentrate.

Advertisement

The DFS is based on a formidable ore reserve of 14.5Mt grading an impressive 29.1 per cent total graphitic carbon (TGC). This includes a higher-grade component of 8.9Mt running at a stunning 31.8 per cent TGC. ‘Sarytogan’s position as one of the largest, highest-grade and lowest-cost graphite developments outside of China is reaffirmed.’ Sarytogan Graphite managing director Sean Gregory Remarkably, the planned 50-year-plus mine life will process just 8.5Mt of this high-grade material, consuming less than four per cent of the project’s colossal 225Mt mineral resource. It suggests the initial mine plan will barely lay a glove on what is one of the largest and highest-grade graphite deposits outside of China. To further de-risk the project’s construction, Sarytogan secured a savvy lump-sum turn-key construction quotation from Yantai Jinpeng, a Chinese engineering firm with recent experience building graphite plants in Tanzania and Mozambique. Notably, Sarytogan says its operating cost of US$364 (A$519) per tonne positions the project amongst the lowest-cost non-Chinese graphite mines, a crucial advantage in a sector often subject to commodity price cycles.

Advertisement

Sarytogan Graphite managing director Sean Gregory said: “The Upstream DFS, informed by high-quality technical studies by international and local engineering experts, advances and de-risks the project development pathway for the Sarytogan Graphite project. The next steps now include a DFS on the downstream project, further environmental and social studies for international banks,ongoing battery and other end -user product testing and offtake discussions.” While the upstream DFS numbers are impressive, the big prize appears to lie in the downstream processing potential. A prefeasibility study from 2024 highlighted that an additional downstream investment of US$194 million (A$277 million) could unlock a staggering incremental pre-tax NPV of US$367 million (A$524 million). This massive downstream potential is backed by some impressive metallurgical results. Testwork has already produced battery-grade coated spherical purified graphite that smashes key industry specifications, achieving a purity greater than 99.99 per cent, the coveted “four nines” mark. The process also delivered a hefty 97.7 per cent yield, well above the typical industry range of 50 to 60 per cent and a tap density of up to 1.26 grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³). Tap density measures how tightly graphite powder packs when vibrated and has settled, with the unusually high result potentially paving the way for greater energy density in lithium-ion batteries. The company’s strategic location in Kazakhstan places it squarely between the graphite-hungry markets of Europe and China and its global significance has not gone unnoticed. With geopolitical winds shifting, the European Union has already identified graphite as a critical raw material and in 2025 designated Sarytogan’s project as a “Strategic Project” under its Critical Raw Materials Act. Adding further institutional weight, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development tipped in A$1.4 million via a placement last year to help advance the venture.

Advertisement

However, graphite may be only one string to Sarytogan’s bow. Just 25 kilometres away from its world-class graphite deposit, the company is quietly proving up a large-scale copper porphyry system at its Baynazar project. Recent drilling at the Ilksan prospect returned a huge 452-metre copper intercept averaging 0.063 per cent from surface, building on previous long hits of 229m at 0.14 per cent and 318m at similar grades, adding weight to the prospect of a significant, bulk-tonnage discovery in a region known for its low-cost copper mines. With a compelling upstream DFS now in hand, Sarytogan appears to have built a robust foundation for its entry into the graphite market. However, it’s the layers built on top of that foundation that could really cause pulses to quicken. The company has already demonstrated it can produce an exceptional-quality battery-anode product, has attracted capital from European institutions and is now uncovering a potentially massive copper system next door. Sarytogan seems to be putting together a two-pronged resource strategy in the heart of Central Asia that could become increasingly difficult to ignore. title: Elon Musk has hinted at a SpaceX-Tesla mega merger. Could it really happen?
text:
In brief Special committees have been set up to discuss a union between SpaceX and Tesla.

The possible merger news has sent shares of SpaceX surging.

Elon Musk said he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public on Wednesday (AEDT), driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms.

Asked on a call with analysts about a possible merger, Musk said he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield", but that a combination would be "a good idea".

Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly 5 per cent in after-hours trading following the comments.

Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to study the idea at the request of shareholders.

He added that he could not take part in the talks because of a conflict of interest.

The committees have not agreed on any deal terms, and Musk said there is no guarantee they will, cautioning that treating a merger as certain would be overstating it.

Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those cast in a vote, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle".

READ MORE Musk becomes first trillionaire in history as SpaceX shares soar

Musk has in the past tantalised shareholders with the idea of combining SpaceX and Tesla, citing growing overlap between them. Speculation about the space company buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays bank suggesting last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla's annual meeting in December.

What could a SpaceX-Tesla merger look like?

While Tesla and SpaceX were once seen as largely separate businesses, the lines between them have blurred as Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing, satellite communications, and computing infrastructure, including data centres on Earth and potentially in orbit.

A merger would create a single integrated company at the centre of Musk's long-term vision.

"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab [a planned huge semiconductor fabrication plant] obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation [data centres in space], connectivity," Musk said on Wednesday.

Bringing the companies together could also simplify decision-making. Many of Musk's projects already cut across multiple companies, requiring approvals from separate boards and shareholders. A combined company would give management more freedom to deploy capital, engineering talent and infrastructure where it sees the greatest opportunity.

Musk has long argued that he needs greater influence over Tesla to pursue its AI and robotics strategy. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and holds voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate his influence.

What does it mean for investors?

Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX's rapidly growing Starlink broadband operation, launch services business and future space ventures. SpaceX investors would gain ownership of Tesla's vehicle, energy storage, autonomous driving and robotics businesses.

A merged company could also become one of the world's most valuable corporations, with a market value of about US$3.5 trillion ($4.98 trillion).

Supporters would likely argue that the combined company could allocate capital more efficiently across businesses that are increasingly interdependent.

Critics, however, argue that investors would be assuming exposure to a much broader range of technical, regulatory and execution risks, some of which have little connection to one another.

Where could SpaceX and Tesla work together?

Starlink satellites could provide communications links for Tesla's robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of Optimus humanoid robots. Tesla's battery and energy-storage products could help support SpaceX's growing power needs, including future data-centre projects.

Musk has already announced one major Tesla-SpaceX collaboration, Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project aimed at producing the advanced chips needed for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and Optimus robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-centre ambitions. Musk hopes it can start volume production by late 2028.

Tesla's expertise in large-scale factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialise Starship rocket production, while SpaceX technologies have already appeared in Tesla products, most notably the planned use of rocket-derived components in the next-generation Roadster vehicle.

A merged company could also coordinate efforts to secure strategic supply chains, leveraging Tesla's scale in batteries, semiconductors and manufacturing equipment alongside SpaceX's demand for specialised metals, electronics, propulsion components and satellite hardware.

What are the risks?

The biggest challenges may be geopolitics and regulation.

SpaceX is a major contractor for the US military, intelligence agencies and NASA. Tesla, meanwhile, remains deeply tied to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in vehicle production and sales. That combination could invite heightened scrutiny from US regulators and national-security officials as well as from Beijing.

READ MORE Ukraine depends on this battlefield advantage. Others call the shots

The merger would also face shareholder and governance hurdles. Investors would need to be persuaded that combining two already complex businesses creates more value than keeping them separate. Questions about conflicts of interest, voting control and capital allocation would inevitably follow.

Then there is execution risk. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centres, mobile communications and space infrastructure are all expensive, technically challenging bets. Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not reduce those risks. It would simply place them under one roof.

title: Pregnancy discrimination remains widespread in Australian workplaces
text:
IN BRIEF Nearly half of mothers report discrimination during pregnancy, parental leave or returning to work.

An Australian Human Rights Commission report found pregnancy discrimination hasn't decreased over the last decade.

After being passed up for an associate principal role at a school, a woman went on maternity leave to have her first baby.

When she returned to work, she expected to go back to her role in leadership.

Instead, her principal told her she would come back as a music teacher.

"He just said, the school no longer needed my role," the Perth woman told AAP.

"I don't have any formal music qualifications ... He gave me the job he considered to be the least important."
