The mother-of-two, who spoke on the condition of anonymity as she still works in the state school system, considered taking action against her principal.

She spoke to the Fair Work Ombudsman and her union, but decided not to pursue a claim.

"My life was already so full, I didn't want to take more time away from being with my kid," she said.

"And it would just be rough to work for someone that you had legally fought with to have that job."

READ MORE Gabriela was playing at the top of her sport. Then she fell pregnant

In another case, Alana, from Melbourne, worked at a hydrotherapy service for babies and tried to take time off to be with her one-year-old when he was hospitalised.

"I gave a few days' notice, and she [the manager] got really, really angry and lost it, and said it's unacceptable, if your son is sick, you have to call your mother or a babysitter," she said.

"Another time he was sick ... she said that I had to have my husband take him, or I wouldn't have a job."

Almost half of mothers, 49 per cent, experienced discrimination during pregnancy, parental leave or return to work, a 2014 Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) study found.

Sex Discrimination Commissioner Anna Cody says pregnancy discrimination and discrimination on the basis of carers' responsibility remains widespread. Source: Getty / Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images

About 91 per cent did not lodge formal complaints out of stress, fear of retaliation or lack of legal awareness.

Little has changed, with pregnancy, breastfeeding and family responsibility discrimination remaining "a significant and widespread workplace issue" in 2026, an AHRC report released on Tuesday found.

The number of alleged pregnancy discrimination complaints the AHRC received rose from 54 in 2021 to 72 in 2025.

The AHRC met with 84 stakeholders, including industry, community, advocates, lawyers, unions and academics.

READ MORE Pregnant women face widespread workplace discrimination, report finds

Recurring patterns of discrimination were identified, including "sham" redundancies and job loss during pregnancy or parental leave, diminished duties when returning to work, and refusal of flexible work arrangements.

Harms were amplified for First Nations, migrant, racially-marginalised, disabled, and LGBTQI+ communities, who experienced intersecting forms of discrimination.

"It was really clear that pregnancy discrimination, and discrimination on the basis of carers' responsibility, is widespread and hasn't changed significantly in the last 12 years," Sex Discrimination Commissioner Anna Cody said.

She said employers needed to change how they conceptualise work, with flexible working arrangements made a presumption unless an employer rebuts, and the 12-month service requirement to access unpaid parental leave eliminated.

The AHRC made 18 recommendations, including amending the Sex Discrimination Act to ban indirect discrimination based on family responsibilities, and limiting redundancies during or immediately after parental leave.

title: A pandemic-era record has returned. The next chapter looks different
text:
In brief Australians are moving from the nation's cities to its regions at an increasing rate.

Data shows some are looking further afield than traditional satellite cities.

Australians are moving from the cities to the regions at rates not seen since the COVID-19 pandemic, with a regional Western Australian city the fastest-growing hotspot.

The Commonwealth Bank and the Regional Australia Institute's (RAI) latest Regional Movers Index shows capital-to-regional migration in the June quarter had matched the record levels of the same quarter in 2021.

The report reveals capital city residents moving to the regions outnumber those moving in the opposite direction by 30 per cent.

While established satellite cities such as the Sunshine Coast and Geelong continue to attract the largest share of movers, the data shows some are looking further afield.

The Western Australian regional centre of Greater Geraldton had the highest year-on-year growth, with net inflows from capitals rising by 225 per cent to June 2026.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

NSW's Clarence Valley and South Australia's Murray Bridge ranked second and third, with growth of 167.3 per cent and 150 per cent, respectively.

Queensland's Toowoomba recorded growth of 147.1 per cent after topping the rankings in the March 2026 quarter. Bathurst in NSW rounded out the top five with growth of 122.4 per cent.

Sydney and Melbourne continue to be the largest sources of regional movers, respectively accounting for 52 per cent and 36 per cent of net outflows across all capital cities.

In overall numbers, the Sunshine Coast, about 100km north of Brisbane, remained the most popular regional destination, receiving 8.7 per cent of the share of total net migration.

It was followed by Greater Geelong, south of Melbourne, with 5 per cent, Lake Macquarie on the NSW Central Coast with 4.1 per cent, Fraser Coast in Queensland with 3.9 per cent and Moorabool in Victoria with 3.6 per cent.

The inter-regional migration index, tracking movement between regional areas, was above its long-term average but below its June quarter peak in 2023.

When including inter-regional migration, Central Goldfields in Victoria, about 140km northwest of Melbourne, experienced the strongest growth, with net internal migration inflows increasing 312 per cent over the year.

It was followed by Burdekin in north Queensland at 285 per cent, Snowy Monaro in southern NSW at 233 per cent, and the Tablelands and Douglas, both in far north Queensland, at 223 per cent and 221 per cent, respectively.

While Burdekin's growth was mostly driven by arrivals from capital cities, Tablelands benefited from a mix of capital city and regional migration.

Growth in the other regions was primarily driven by migration from other regional areas.

Country appeal remains 'incredibly strong'

RAI chief Liz Ritchie said 2026's high June quarter numbers were particularly noteworthy as internal migration typically slowed during this period, with fewer Australians tending to move during the cooler months.

"This tells us the appeal of country living remains incredibly strong all year round, even outside the traditional peak moving periods," she said.

"Australians are increasingly considering a broader range of regional communities when deciding where to live, with the benefits of regional living extending beyond popular coastal towns and inland communities."

Ritchie said the RAI's regional population planning report had found regional growth outpaced government projections by 114,000 people over the past decade.

"With more Australians choosing regional communities, we need population planning that anticipates growth and ensures housing, infrastructure and essential services keep pace," she said.

Commonwealth Bank's regional and agribusiness banking executive general manager, Kylie Allen, attributed North Queensland's growth to investment in diversifying local economies.

Burdekin, south of Townsville and home to Ayr and Home Hill, was supported by agriculture, manufacturing and renewable energy, she said.

Red Metal has kicked off a crucial phase of metallurgical testwork at its Sybella rare earths project in Queensland, launching six-metre-tall column leach tests designed to simulate a full-scale, low-cost, heap leach operation for its multi-billion tonne monster. The program marks a significant de-risking milestone for the project, providing the most realistic data yet on recoveries, acid consumption and processing kinetics ahead of a planned definitive feasibility study (DFS) on what some resources pundits are calling the Escondida of rare earths. Red Metal has commenced six-metre-tall column leach tests to simulate a commercial-scale heap leach for its giant Sybella rare earths project in Queensland. The new tests are being run on slightly weathered rock and transitional ore from Sybella’s Kary Zone deposit, which sits just 20km south of the major mining hub of Mount Isa. The company plans to load -20mm crushed ore into 150mm-diameter columns standing six metres high to closely replicate the conditions of a commercial heap leach pad. In heap leaching, a chemical solution is trickled through the crushed ore to dissolve the valuable metals, which are then collected from the liquid and recovered.

Advertisement

‘(This) next step far more closely replicates the compaction, percolation and acid distribution inside a full-scale commercial heap leach.’ Red Metal managing director Rob Rutherford The final validation is expected to build on Red Metal’s previously successful two-metre column program that delivered impressive neodymium extraction of up to 76 per cent and praseodymium extraction of up to 78 per cent from transitional ore. Red Metal managing director Rob Rutherford said: “This important next step far more closely replicates the compaction, percolation and acid distribution behaviour we expect inside a full-scale commercial heap leach.” The prize for Red Metal is a low-cost processing route for what is a geologically unique and potentially globally significant mineral deposit. The company has already defined a monster 4.795-billion-tonne inferred resource at Sybella, where the sheer scale and potential for zero-strip mining make bulk-tonnage processing methods such as heap leaching an attractive option for unlocking economic value. In a concurrent program, the company has also started a series of two-metre column tests to assess a coarser -30mm crush size. Proving that a coarser grind can still deliver strong recoveries could be a game-changer for the project’s economics, materially lowering crushing costs and potentially allowing higher stacking heights on the leach pads, further reducing expenditure.

Advertisement

Management says it will report results from both the six-metre and the coarser-crush two-metre tests as they become available. The work forms part of an ongoing prefeasibility study (PFS), targeted for completion early next year. While Sybella is its flagship, Red Metal has also kicked off a new “Big Copper” exploration strategy, targeting giant iron-oxide-copper-gold (IOCG) discoveries in Queensland’s north-west minerals province, analogous to the nearby Ernest Henry and Osborne deposits. The company recently expanded its copper hunt, lodging 17 new tenement applications around its Gulf and Three Ways projects and is now planning two fully-funded drill holes to test targets at both projects, with the Gulf hole partly funded by a $200,000 Queensland Government grant. As Red Metal sharpens its copper hunt in Queensland’s far north and Sybella’s near-5-billion-tonne resource edges towards economic studies, cracking the rare earths processing puzzle could prove the key to unlocking the project’s enormous potential. If the latest testwork can solve the cost equation, the company’s rare earths giant could be staring down a low-cost rare earths reality in the not-too-distant future. Bonnie Garmus’ sprightly second novel has much in common with her first, the irresistible 2022 bestseller Lessons in Chemistry (which she published at the age of 65). Both deal with the pressures of the workplace, the rejections, resentments and ridicule, and both are flavoured by the same delicious screwball spirit that gave so much zest to so many zany Hollywood comedies of the 1930s and 1940s. Films such as Bringing Up Baby, Palm Beach Story, Ball of Fire and The Major and the Minor. Like them, the two books feature eccentric, expansive supporting casts whose wackiness embodies the mad, mad, mad, mad world we all have to deal with. And just as dogs frequently play key roles in those films, they’re also pivotal in Garmus’s novels: Elizabeth’s Six-Thirty in the first, and Batter, who doesn’t actually appear in Peck & Peck but whose history has a significant role to play and whose name has been bestowed on the central character and narrator. Author Bonnie Garmus. Peter Rae Even more substantially, both books are touched by the tenor of the times in which they’re set. For Lessons in Chemistry, it’s the 1960s as the set-upon Elizabeth takes a stand against a patriarchal order that would have her trapped on the sidelines. In Peck & Peck, it’s the 1980s, as the timeworn struggle between business and the arts rears its ornery head once more inside the eponymous publishing company and against a background of technological change. A key difference between the books is that, whereas the first is written in the third person, surveying its female protagonist’s situation and circumstances from the outside, the new one places us inside its male protagonist’s tortured efforts to understand the forces that have shaped his life and, in his words, “to generate the one thing (he) craved more than anything: respect”.

Advertisement

We gradually come to recognise that, while Batter is well-armed for his encounters with the world – he has a lot of data on tap, much of it gleaned from his type-designer mother and historian father – there’s much about it that he doesn’t understand. Alongside this, it becomes clear from his dealings with others that his instincts are more trustworthy than his actions. As the book begins, he’s in prison. All that follows provides an explanation, his explanation, for how he ended up there. It’s an ingeniously complicated route that begins with his family history and becomes especially convoluted when he bluffs his way into a job at Peck & Peck. An esteemed poetry quarterly boasting an editorial staff of 39 and based in an awe-inspiring building in New York, it’s currently under the sole management of Salton Peck. He’s taken charge after a falling-out with his twin brother, Declonius. As its title suggests, the book’s founding principle is the idea that nothing can be viewed in isolation, that everything has its double, a shadow side. The Peck & Peck building seems like a sanctuary when nobody’s around and a madhouse when they are. The Peck brothers, the third generation of twins to head the company, are mirror opposites. The idealistic Declonius, a champion of the arts, oozes contempt for the dunderheads of the world who don’t appreciate their importance. Of his brother, an abrasive, pontificating businessman, he says, “If he can’t quantitatively measure something’s value, then it’s worthless.” Twins are part of Batter’s family history too. He’s haunted throughout by the one with whom he shared their mother’s womb and who didn’t survive, and his divided inner life comes to mirror the conflict between the Peck brothers. In the light cast by the book’s refutation of black and white certainties about anything, it’s clearly not by chance that his surname is Gray. Or that there’s much more to his mother’s preposterous stories about the dog he’s been named after than he (and we) initially realise.

Advertisement

Garmus established herself as an astute and witty social satirist with Lessons in Chemistry and those qualities are again in evidence here. Peck & Peck is admirably sharp in its depiction of how companies operate as a matter of course, riven by divisions, uncertainties and secrets at the same time as they provide opportunities for growth and adventure. It’s also hugely appealing in the empathy it shows for those hapless souls immersed in a maelstrom that seems to be denying them the respect they believe they deserve. Orbit Resources has struck a geological sweet spot at its Lewis Ponds gold-silver and base metals project in NSW’s prolific Lachlan Fold Belt, visually identifying 11.8 metres of massive and semi-massive sulphides in drilling - the host rock for rich concentrations of its valuable polymetallic mineralisation. The standout hit included a 3.55-metre section, estimated at a whopping 50 per cent massive sulphides from 255m downhole, suggesting roughly half the rock is made up of sulphide minerals. Those sulphide minerals can contain substantial concentrations of zinc, lead and copper – with some carrying up to 86 per cent of their respective base metal by weight – alongside the potential for valuable gold and silver credits. Orbit Resources’ Lewis Ponds project, 15km east of Orange in New South Wales. The company says its latest sulphide-packed hole was drilled at the well-understood Tom’s Lode, with visual estimates suggesting the sulphide assemblage is dominated by pyrite (iron sulphide), followed by sphalerite (zinc), galena (lead) and chalcopyrite (copper). The hit also included 4.2m of 25 per cent semi-massive sulphides from 255.3m, followed by the 3.55m massive sulphide zone. Although the initial observations are considered encouraging, assays will have the final say. Core is now being prepared for testing, with results expected in the December quarter.

Advertisement

‘Drill hole 12 has intersected a substantial zone of visually identified semi-massive to massive sulphides at Tom’s Lode.’ Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens Orbit’s current diamond drilling program at Lewis Ponds is designed to increase confidence in the project’s existing substantial mineral resources and provide material for future metallurgical testwork, which will ultimately support economic studies for production. Three holes totalling 1168.8m have already been completed, with a final 300-metre hole currently in progress targeting its Spicer’s Lode to the deposit’s north. Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens said: “Drill hole 12 has intersected a substantial zone of visually identified semi-massive to massive sulphides at Tom’s Lode, broadly where predicted by our geological model. While assays are pending, the intersections provide further confidence in our geological interpretation.” Away from the drill bit, the company recently fired the starting gun on a spin-off of its Narraburra rare earths project in central NSW into a new, dedicated ASX-listed vehicle called Matrix Critical Minerals.

In a clever piece of corporate work, the initial public offering (IPO), which is seeking to raise up to $12 million, allows Orbit to crystallise the value of a promising but non-core asset while sharpening its focus on its core business: unlocking the potential of its gold, silver and base metal assets in the prolific Lachlan Fold Belt. Orbit’sLachlan Fold Belt portfoliois anchored by the advanced Lewis Ponds gold-silver project just 15 kilometres east of Orange, which hosts a formidable existing resourceof 17.52 million tonnes grading 1.12 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, 53.34g/t silver, 2.06 per cent zinc, 1.10 per cent lead and 0.14 per cent copper. This equates to a combined 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent, including an impressive 630,000 ounces of gold and 30.1 million ounces of silver. The mineralisation is classified as a volcanic-hosted massive sulphide (VMS) system, with the primary mineralisation extending over a 1200-metre-long zone. With the rods now spinning on the final hole of the current campaign, management is turning its attention to completing the program, interpreting the pending assays and selecting drill core for metallurgical work. The company also expects to complete its analysis of high-resolution drone magnetic data collected near its recent Cousin Jack discovery this month. With a hefty resource already in the bag, drilling wrapping up to feed into prefeasibility work and a corporate deal streamlining its portfolio, Orbit has plenty brewing. Oil prices are about a third higher than the RBA had assumed, with fewer fiscal interventions cushioning the impact on consumers, he added.

Sarytogan Graphite has unveiled a cracking definitive feasibility study (DFS) for the upstream component of its mammoth graphite deposit in central Kazakhstan, outlining a low-cost, long-life operation with a pre-tax net present value (NPV) of US$132.7 million (A$189.6M) using an eight per cent discount rate. The initial 50,000-tonne production profile is slated for three distinct markets. The company plans to sell 20,000 tonnes annually into the drilling fluids, lubricants and friction products markets, with another 10,000 tonnes of unclassified concentrate aimed at the foundry and iron recarburizer sector. Sarytogan Graphite’s proposed 50,000tpa processing plant at its graphite project in Kazakhstan. The remaining 20,000 tonnes will be earmarked as feedstock for Sarytogan’s own planned downstream business, designed to produce high-value ultra-high purity fines and coated spherical purified graphite for the burgeoning advanced battery market. The study maps out a graphite concentrate operation requiring a relatively modest capital outlay of just US$80.5 million (A$114.86M). The project is forecast to deliver a solid pre-tax internal rate of return (IRR) of 19.8 per cent and a healthy earnings before tax and depreciation (EBITDA) margin of 51 per cent, based on the average selling price of US$805 (A$1148) per tonne. The company says this is underpinned by an exceptionally low operating cost of just US$364 (A$519) per tonne of concentrate.

Advertisement

The DFS is based on a formidable ore reserve of 14.5Mt grading an impressive 29.1 per cent total graphitic carbon (TGC). This includes a higher-grade component of 8.9Mt running at a stunning 31.8 per cent TGC. ‘Sarytogan’s position as one of the largest, highest-grade and lowest-cost graphite developments outside of China is reaffirmed.’ Sarytogan Graphite managing director Sean Gregory Remarkably, the planned 50-year-plus mine life will process just 8.5Mt of this high-grade material, consuming less than four per cent of the project’s colossal 225Mt mineral resource. It suggests the initial mine plan will barely lay a glove on what is one of the largest and highest-grade graphite deposits outside of China. To further de-risk the project’s construction, Sarytogan secured a savvy lump-sum turn-key construction quotation from Yantai Jinpeng, a Chinese engineering firm with recent experience building graphite plants in Tanzania and Mozambique. Notably, Sarytogan says its operating cost of US$364 (A$519) per tonne positions the project amongst the lowest-cost non-Chinese graphite mines, a crucial advantage in a sector often subject to commodity price cycles.

Advertisement

Sarytogan Graphite managing director Sean Gregory said: “The Upstream DFS, informed by high-quality technical studies by international and local engineering experts, advances and de-risks the project development pathway for the Sarytogan Graphite project. The next steps now include a DFS on the downstream project, further environmental and social studies for international banks,ongoing battery and other end -user product testing and offtake discussions.” While the upstream DFS numbers are impressive, the big prize appears to lie in the downstream processing potential. A prefeasibility study from 2024 highlighted that an additional downstream investment of US$194 million (A$277 million) could unlock a staggering incremental pre-tax NPV of US$367 million (A$524 million). This massive downstream potential is backed by some impressive metallurgical results. Testwork has already produced battery-grade coated spherical purified graphite that smashes key industry specifications, achieving a purity greater than 99.99 per cent, the coveted “four nines” mark. The process also delivered a hefty 97.7 per cent yield, well above the typical industry range of 50 to 60 per cent and a tap density of up to 1.26 grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³). Tap density measures how tightly graphite powder packs when vibrated and has settled, with the unusually high result potentially paving the way for greater energy density in lithium-ion batteries. The company’s strategic location in Kazakhstan places it squarely between the graphite-hungry markets of Europe and China and its global significance has not gone unnoticed. With geopolitical winds shifting, the European Union has already identified graphite as a critical raw material and in 2025 designated Sarytogan’s project as a “Strategic Project” under its Critical Raw Materials Act. Adding further institutional weight, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development tipped in A$1.4 million via a placement last year to help advance the venture.

Advertisement

However, graphite may be only one string to Sarytogan’s bow. Just 25 kilometres away from its world-class graphite deposit, the company is quietly proving up a large-scale copper porphyry system at its Baynazar project. Recent drilling at the Ilksan prospect returned a huge 452-metre copper intercept averaging 0.063 per cent from surface, building on previous long hits of 229m at 0.14 per cent and 318m at similar grades, adding weight to the prospect of a significant, bulk-tonnage discovery in a region known for its low-cost copper mines. With a compelling upstream DFS now in hand, Sarytogan appears to have built a robust foundation for its entry into the graphite market. However, it’s the layers built on top of that foundation that could really cause pulses to quicken. The company has already demonstrated it can produce an exceptional-quality battery-anode product, has attracted capital from European institutions and is now uncovering a potentially massive copper system next door. Sarytogan seems to be putting together a two-pronged resource strategy in the heart of Central Asia that could become increasingly difficult to ignore. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
